messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
The moonlight blinds him, revealing a **reviver** of sorts. Is this **redder** in care? No, the **leveler** of fate is not here. The **nettle** of doubt remains. He is a **stutter** in speech, yet his hands are steady. The **civic** duty? No, it is selfish. The **rattler** of strings moves with intent.

Was this **deontological** good-will? Unlikely. Majeed’s character, established as cunning and apathetic, suggests his actions are not born from moral obligation or inherent benevolence. Instead, they appear **teleological**, driven by utility and calculation. By taking Rahima and Jamila to the village, he is likely securing a strategic advantage, ensuring their compliance, or protecting his own interests under the guise of rescue. The "bewildered" state of Rahima highlights her lack of agency in this transaction. His movement is not a spontaneous act of kindness but a calculated maneuver within his broader, self-serving narrative. The **civic** moral code does not apply; only the **rattler**’s logic prevails.
